1.explanation: All of the code-path modeling for logical operators (&&, ||, ??) lives in code-path-analysis/code-path-analyzer.js.  This file is responsible for listening to AST “LogicalExpression” events and forking/joining segments to represent short-circuit behavior.  Because the AND (`&&`) case and the nullish-coalescing (`??`) case are both handled there, and because no other place in ESLint’s code manipulates the shape of code-path segments for logical operators, this is the only file that needs to be corrected to insert the missing branch from the falsy-`a` fork directly to the `c` evaluation path.
1.bug_scenario:
When you write a nested logical AND combined with a nullish-coalescing operator — for example

    (a && b) ?? c

ESLint’s code-path analyzer should model the fact that if `a` is falsy you skip both `b` and the `&&` and immediately fall through to evaluate `c` (because `(null && b) ?? c` only runs `c`).  The current graph (and DOT/image) only shows two branches: one through `b` into `c`, and one that skips both into the final exit node — but the branch from the `a` node directly into the nullish side (`c`) is missing.  That missing edge means any rules that depend on accurate code-path info (e.g. “was `c` definitely run when `a` is falsy?”) will be incorrect.

In short: `(a && b) ?? c` is being treated like `(a || b) ?? c` for path-forking purposes, and that leads to a lost branch where `a`→`c` (on falsy `a`) should be.

2.explanation:
Both of these files are at the heart of ESLint’s code-path analysis. 

1. lib/linter/code-path-analysis/code-path-analyzer.js  
   • This is where ESLint hooks into the AST events for LogicalExpression and decides how to fork or skip evaluation of the left or right side based on the operator (‘&&’, ‘||’, and in this case ‘??’). The existing logic treats ‘??’ exactly like ‘||’, so it never creates the branch that runs c when the left side (a && b) short-circuits on a nullish a.  

2. lib/linter/code-path-analysis/fork-context.js  
   • This module tracks the stack of nested forks (if, ?:, &&, ||, etc.) and remembers which branch you’re on so that, on exit, it can reconnect the right segments. Because ‘??’ is lumped together with the other logical operators, it doesn’t push/pop a separate fork context of its own and thus cannot generate the “a → c” branch. 

Fixing the logic in these two files to treat `??` specially—so that if the left operand to the nullish coalesce is itself a short-circuited `&&` we still create a segment that evaluates `c` directly—will restore the missing code-path branch.
2.bug_scenario:
When you run code-path analysis on the expression “(a && b) ?? c”, ESLint builds a control-flow graph that perfectly matches “(a || b) ?? c” instead of the intended “&& then nullish coalesce.” In particular you never get the direct path “a → c” (skipping b) that you need when a is null or undefined. The DOT diagram and screenshot show only three routes: 
  • a true → b → c → exit
  • a false → exit (no c)
  • b true → exit (no c)
But in reality, if a is nullish, you should go from a straight into c without even touching b. That branch is missing.
